articles.title: White House rolls out AI funding — and signals a new era for US science
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 24 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02332-8Chief US science adviser calls for a shakeup in funding while handing out grants to accelerate research with AI.
articles.content:
Michael Kratsios, chief science adviser to US President Donald Trump, released a report this week that reimagines how science in the country is funded. Credit: Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty

Washington DC

It was a big week for science in the administration of US President Donald Trump. On Tuesday, the president’s chief science adviser, Michael Kratsios, release a report called Science: A New Golden Age that proposes substantial changes to federally funded research. The next day saw him help to unveil some of the first winners of research grants from the Genesis Mission, the administration’s flagship artificial-intelligence initiative.

For the past year and a half, the Republican-led administration has made headlines for attempting to cut funding for US science that it disfavours. This week’s events are notable because they move forward the science that it does favour — in particular, AI.

Trump has big AI and quantum ambitions: this scientist’s job is to make them reality

Some 5,000 teams applied for funding from the Genesis Mission, which the administration billed as a programme “comparable in urgency and ambition to the Manhattan Project” to accelerate US science with AI. At a summit on 22 July, officials announced about 280 winning projects in a first phase of the programme. Teams will apply AI to problems such as improving the US power grid and automating laboratories, and will receive a 9-month grant for between US$500,000 and $750,000. Researchers in these teams can also submit applications for a second phase: a three-year programme involving millions in annual funding.

“I was very, very, very happy” to be chosen “because it was incredibly competitive,” winner Jeremy Zucker told Nature at the summit. Zucker, a computational scientist at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory in Richland, Washington, is leading a project that will model algal growth in ponds to maximize biofuel production.

Kratsios’s report got a more mixed reception at a hearing in Washington DC that he attended on the same day. In the report, he calls for shifting US science funding away from “legacy institutions” such as universities. “Too much of our research enterprise has come to serve itself rather than the scientists within it,” he wrote. Under this new vision, individual scientists would be supported by programmes such as ‘golden tickets’, which give grant reviewers the ability to override the decisions of their colleagues to fund high-risk proposals. “We should be testing other ways to make breakthroughs than what we’ve been doing for so many years,” he said at the hearing of the US House of Representatives Committee on Science, Space and Technology. He argued that US science is stagnating and needs to be rethought.

Members of the US Congress, who decide what science to fund, had mixed reactions. Republicans on the committee broadly expressed support for Kratsios’s vision for US science; Democrats, however, criticized the Trump administration’s cuts to science budgets and agencies, as well as its push to take political control of grant awards. “You aren’t launching us into ‘the golden age of innovation’. You’re sending us back to the Stone Age,” said Gabe Amo, a Democrat representing Rhode Island.

Some scientists have been quick to criticize the report. Carl Bergstrom, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Washington in Seattle, wrote on the social-media platform Bluesky that the administration seems determined to “destroy” US universities. (Trump and his Republican allies have accused US research institutions of being discriminatory towards conservative views, and the administration has withheld funding from some universities, citing antisemitism.)

Grant challenges

Lawmakers also questioned Kratsios about media reports, including one from Nature, that the US National Science Foundation (NSF) plans to claw back about $500 million from its grant-making divisions and funnelling the money towards a new White House initiative. Democrat Zoe Lofgren of California queried the chief science adviser about this. He responded: “I’m not familiar with those details. I would refer you to NSF,” but made the case that the United States should “be more deliberative and specific about trying to tackle grand challenges”.

NSF plans cuts to core science programmes to fund White House initiative

Nature has learnt that the NSF has now pulled back $300 million from two of its divisions: mathematics and physical sciences, and computer and information science and engineering. Programme officers, who handle grant proposals at the NSF, have pulled back 150 proposals that have already passed peer review to free up the money, which was allotted to the agency by the US Congress. Some proposals have been rescinded, others have had funding cuts and still others have been held until the next fiscal year.

Staff members at the NSF, who spoke to Nature on the condition of anonymity out of fear of reprisals, say the money is probably going to a programme called Grand Research Challenges, organized by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, which Kratsios runs. A preliminary document shown to Nature that appears to outline the challenges lists four areas: the future of intelligence, the frontier of quantum phenomena, advanced materials and matter and the foundations of biological design.

A spokesperson for the NSF said that the agency would not comment on internal budget deliberations. They said that funds for research activities in fiscal year 2026 could be awarded that year or the next one, and that "NSF revises budgets and manages portfolios as needed".
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant new US government initiative to accelerate scientific research in artificial intelligence through substantial funding and innovative grant mechanisms. This has broad societal implications by potentially advancing AI technology that could improve infrastructure and biofuel production. Despite some controversy and political debate, the focus on boosting high-risk, high-reward science funding marks a meaningful and inspiring shift in science policy with potential large-scale benefits.
articles.personality_title: US launches major AI research funding to speed up science
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context**  
The US government has been debating how to best support scientific research. Recently, some parts of science funding faced cuts, but new efforts are focusing on boosting research in artificial intelligence (AI), a technology that can help solve big problems.

**What happened**  
In July 2026, Michael Kratsios, the chief science adviser to President Trump, released a report called "Science: A New Golden Age". It suggests changing how US science funding works, moving away from traditional universities and supporting more risky but promising projects. At the same time, the government announced winners of the Genesis Mission grants, a new AI research program. About 280 teams won grants ranging from $500,000 to $750,000 for nine months to use AI on projects like improving the power grid and biofuel production.

**Impact**  
This new funding program is important because it focuses on AI, which can improve many areas like energy and the environment. For example, one winning project will use AI to grow algae better for biofuel, a cleaner energy source. The approach also encourages scientists to try bold ideas that might lead to big discoveries, rather than just safe, usual research. This could speed up science in new directions.

**What's next step**  
Teams that win the first phase can apply for a second phase with multi-year funding worth millions of dollars. The government will watch closely to see which projects make real progress. Meanwhile, debates continue in Congress about how science funding should be managed and whether the new ideas will work well.

**One-sentence takeaway**  
The US government has launched a new AI-focused funding program aiming to support bold scientific research and speed up important discoveries in technology and energy.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les États-Unis lancent un important financement pour la recherche en IA afin d’accélérer la science
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte**  
Le gouvernement américain débat sur la meilleure façon de soutenir la recherche scientifique. Récemment, certains financements ont été réduits, mais de nouvelles initiatives se concentrent sur la recherche en intelligence artificielle (IA), une technologie qui peut aider à résoudre de grands problèmes.

**Ce qui s'est passé**  
En juillet 2026, Michael Kratsios, conseiller scientifique principal du président Trump, a publié un rapport intitulé « Science : un nouvel âge d’or ». Il propose de changer la manière dont le financement de la science est attribué, en s’éloignant des universités traditionnelles et en soutenant des projets plus risqués mais prometteurs. En même temps, le gouvernement a annoncé les gagnants des subventions de la mission Genesis, un nouveau programme de recherche en IA. Environ 280 équipes ont reçu des subventions de 500 000 à 750 000 dollars pour neuf mois afin d’utiliser l’IA sur des projets comme l’amélioration du réseau électrique et la production de biocarburants.

**Impact**  
Ce nouveau programme de financement est important car il se concentre sur l’IA, qui peut améliorer de nombreux domaines tels que l’énergie et l’environnement. Par exemple, un projet gagnant utilisera l’IA pour mieux cultiver des algues destinées aux biocarburants, une source d’énergie plus propre. Cette approche encourage aussi les scientifiques à tenter des idées audacieuses qui pourraient conduire à de grandes découvertes, plutôt que de se limiter à des recherches classiques. Cela pourrait accélérer la science dans de nouvelles directions.

**Prochaine étape**  
Les équipes gagnantes de la première phase peuvent postuler à une seconde phase avec un financement pluriannuel de plusieurs millions de dollars. Le gouvernement surveillera de près les projets qui feront de réels progrès. Par ailleurs, les débats continuent au Congrès sur la gestion du financement scientifique et sur l’efficacité des nouvelles idées.

**Résumé en une phrase**  
Le gouvernement américain a lancé un nouveau programme de financement axé sur l’IA pour soutenir des recherches scientifiques audacieuses et accélérer les découvertes importantes en technologie et énergie.
articles.personality_title_es: EE. UU. lanza un gran financiamiento para investigación en IA para acelerar la ciencia
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto**  
El gobierno de Estados Unidos ha estado debatiendo cómo apoyar mejor la investigación científica. Recientemente, algunos fondos para la ciencia se redujeron, pero ahora hay nuevos esfuerzos para impulsar la investigación en inteligencia artificial (IA), una tecnología que puede ayudar a resolver grandes problemas.

**Qué pasó**  
En julio de 2026, Michael Kratsios, asesor científico principal del presidente Trump, publicó un informe llamado "Ciencia: Una nueva edad dorada". Propone cambiar cómo se financia la ciencia en EE. UU., alejándose de las universidades tradicionales y apoyando proyectos más arriesgados pero prometedores. Al mismo tiempo, el gobierno anunció a los ganadores de las becas de la Misión Génesis, un nuevo programa de investigación en IA. Unas 280 equipos recibieron becas de entre 500,000 y 750,000 dólares por nueve meses para usar IA en proyectos como mejorar la red eléctrica y la producción de biocombustibles.

**Impacto**  
Este nuevo programa de financiamiento es importante porque se centra en la IA, que puede mejorar muchas áreas como la energía y el medio ambiente. Por ejemplo, un proyecto ganador usará IA para cultivar algas mejor para producir biocombustibles, una fuente de energía más limpia. Este enfoque también anima a los científicos a probar ideas audaces que podrían llevar a grandes descubrimientos, en lugar de solo investigaciones seguras y comunes. Esto podría acelerar la ciencia en nuevas direcciones.

**Próximo paso**  
Los equipos que ganen la primera fase pueden solicitar una segunda fase con financiamiento de varios años y millones de dólares. El gobierno observará de cerca qué proyectos logran avances reales. Mientras tanto, continúan los debates en el Congreso sobre cómo debe manejarse el financiamiento científico y si las nuevas ideas funcionarán bien.

**Frase clave**  
El gobierno de EE. UU. ha lanzado un nuevo programa de financiamiento centrado en IA para apoyar investigaciones audaces y acelerar descubrimientos importantes en tecnología y energía.
